note: Single home for the House of Mendes evidence records. mendes/map/app-1.js fetches this file for the map and journeys viewers; the planned claims reader consumes it too. The court array is generated by scripts/build_mendes_court_claims.py from mendes/data/ptolemaic-queens-fragments.json — edit the mapping there, not the records here. Every other section is hand-maintained here.

claims.cite: Pliny, Naturalis historia 12.107; compare Dioscorides, De materia medica 1.59.1, 3.83–84
claims.note: Pliny says hammoniacum exudes in the sands of Africa near the oracle of Hammon from a tree called metopon. Dioscorides instead assigns metopon to the galbanum plant and treats ammoniacum separately. This is a competing ancient etymological and provenance claim—not a Metopion ingredient. The point conventionally anchors the oracle at Siwa; no supply route is inferred and no modern taxon is imposed.

court.cite: Galen, De compositione medicamentorum secundum locos, Kühn 12.403.15–404.2

source.digitalLocator: TLG 0057:076, book 1, lines corresponding to Kühn 12.403.15–404.2

court.commentary: This selected formula is followed by Galen's own modification and efficacy report. The larger Cleopatra alopecia cluster continues through Kühn 12.405.17 with multiple variants. It is important evidence for recipe transmission under Cleopatra's name, but this selection has no olfactory content.

court.subtype: medical-cosmetic: hair-growth salve with odor masking
court.cite: Galen, De compositione medicamentorum secundum locos, Kühn 12.432.12–433.2

source.section: To generate hair on the head
source.digitalLocator: TLG 0057:076, book 1, lines corresponding to Kühn 12.432.12–433.2

court.commentary: This is the strongest Galenic example for the olfactory question. Smell is treated as an undesirable property of a therapeutic cosmetic, and wine is added as an odor-management step rather than as a luxury perfume. The larger Cleopatra hair cluster continues through Kühn 12.434.2.

court.cite: Galen, De compositione medicamentorum secundum locos, Kühn 12.492.6–13

source.section: Remedies for achōrai of the scalp
source.digitalLocator: TLG 0057:076, book 1, lines corresponding to Kühn 12.492.6–13

court.commentary: A genuine sequence of washing, smearing, and covering. Myrtle and wine-oil are potentially aromatic, but the text makes no claim about fragrance; the olfactory relevance is therefore indirect. This is the first selection from a longer Cleopatra cluster at Kühn 12.492.6–493.12.

court.subtype: medical-cosmetic: hair curling, darkening, and softening
court.cite: Paul of Aegina, Epitomae medicae libri septem, 3.2.1; Heiberg 132.1–15
court.commentary: Paul preserves a cluster of variants under Cleopatra's name. Myrtle unguent and myrtle oil make the dossier relevant to scented cosmetics, although the stated objectives are texture and color, not smell.

court.subtype: medical-cosmetic: falling hair and skin lesions
court.cite: Aetius of Amida, Iatricorum libri V–VIII, 6.56.27–34
court.commentary: A fully procedural medical cosmetic, including preparation, storage, application, interval, humoral indication, and an additional dermatological use. It is a later witness to a recipe also transmitted in Galen's Cleopatra section. Wine is functional; fragrance is not mentioned.

court.cite: Aetius of Amida, Iatricorum libri V–VIII, 8.6.31–34

source.subsection: Another costly fragrant cleanser of Queen Cleopatra

court.commentary: The clearest queen-attributed perfume recipe in the medical corpus: its heading calls the preparation both costly and fragrant, and the ingredient list is dominated by aromatics. It is a powdered cleanser rather than an oil perfume.

court.cite: Galen, De compositione medicamentorum secundum locos, Kühn 12.446.1–4

source.digitalLocator: TLG 0057:076, book 1, lines corresponding to Kühn 12.446.1–4

court.commentary: This is a report about textual or pharmaceutical transmission, not a recipe. It supports Cleopatra's place in a later medical genealogy but says nothing about perfume or smell.

court.cite: Athenaeus, quoting Apollonius of Tyre, Deipnosophistae, Kaibel 523.20–23
court.commentary: This is a report, not a formulation. It is the dossier's most direct evidence that royal women were remembered as patrons of perfume production and that Berenice's reign was used to periodize Cyrenaic rose perfume.

court.subtype: court poetry and perfumed royal body

source.digitalLocator: TLG 0533:003, epigram 51, lines 1–4; TLG 0533:004, book 5, epigram 146

court.commentary: The perfume is poetic, not a recipe or documentary court record. It makes the newly fashioned queen a living fourth Grace whose scented body signals divine beauty and Ptolemaic abundance.
A report of deliberately engineered smell in Cleopatra's Aphrodite-like river spectacle. The incense extends the royal performance beyond the barge into the surrounding landscape.
This is experimental toxicology in narrative form, not a recipe and not olfactory evidence. It is retained because later discussions often blur Cleopatra's drug lore with perfume lore.

court.cite: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia, 21.9.12; Mayhoff 384.3–11 for the selected excerpt

source.editionTitle: C. Plini Secundi Naturalis historiae libri XXXVII

court.commentary: The crown is a scented social object, but Pliny does not give a poison formula. The anecdote depends on the sensory and convivial plausibility of flower garlands while presenting Cleopatra as a demonstrator of hidden toxicity.

court.subtype: epic representation of a perfumed banquet

source.editionTitle: M. Annaei Lucani Belli civilis libri decem

court.commentary: Epic narrative, not a court inventory or recipe. Lucan makes aroma a marker of immediacy, import, excess, and Alexandria's access to luxury supply chains.

court.cite: Florus, Epitome de Tito Livio bellorum omnium annorum DCC libri duo, 2.21.11 (= 4.11.11)

source.ancientWork: Epitome de Tito Livio bellorum omnium annorum DCC libri duo
source.digitalLocator: PHI Latin LAT1242, book 2, chapter 21, section 11

court.commentary: This compressed historiographical tableau makes fragrance part of Cleopatra's royal self-presentation in death. It is a literary report, not evidence for a particular aromatic formula.

court.cite: Josephus, Antiquitates Judaicae, 15.96; TLG chapter 96, line 6
court.commentary: Not a perfume recipe but economic evidence: Herod leased from Cleopatra revenues attached to a uniquely prized aromatic crop. Josephus, Jewish War 1.361 supplies a close parallel, saying Antony gave her the Jericho palm grove where balsam grows.

court.subtype: royal procession, incense, and aromatic display
court.cite: Athenaeus, quoting Callixenus of Rhodes, Deipnosophistae, Kaibel 448.16–17; 449.7–9; 449.24–25

source.quotedSource: Callixenus of Rhodes, On Alexandria, book 1

court.commentary: These details belong to one Ptolemaic procession but should not be collapsed into a claim that Berenice personally supplied the aromatics. The evidence is for a queen's cult monument embedded in a spectacle saturated with incense and aromatic wealth.
